class/CollectionService.d:
CollectionService manages groups (collections) of instances with tags. Tags are sets of strings applied to instances that replicate from the server to the client. They are also serialized when places are saved.

The primary use of CollectionService is to register instances with specific tags that you can use to extend their behavior. If you find yourself adding the same script to many different instances, a script that uses CollectionService may be better.

Tags can be added or removed through this class' methods such as AddTag() or RemoveTag(). They can also be managed directly in Studio through the Tags section of an instance's properties.

Replication

When tags replicate, all tags on an instance replicate at the same time. Therefore, if you set a tag on an instance from the client then add/remove a different tag on the same instance from the server, the client's local tags on the instance are overwritten. In StreamingEnabled places, instances can be unloaded as they leave the client's streamed area. If such an instance re-enters the streamed area, properties and tags will be re-synchronized from the server. This can cause changes made by LocalScripts to be overwritten/removed.
class/CollectionService.s: A service which manages instance collections using assigned tags.

m.d:
This method applies a tag to an Instance, doing nothing if the tag is already applied to that instance. Successfully adding a tag will fire a signal created by GetInstanceAddedSignal() with the given tag.

Warnings

  • An instance's tags that were added client-side will be dropped if the server later adds or removes a tag on that instance because the server replicates all tags together and overwrites previous tags.

  • When tagging an instance, it is common that some resources are used to give the tag its functionality, for example event connections or tables. To prevent memory leaks, it's a good idea to clean these up (disconnect, set to nil, etc.) when no longer needed for a tag. Do this when calling RemoveTag(), calling Instance:Destroy() or in a function connected to a signal returned by GetInstanceRemovedSignal().
m.s: Applies a tag to an `Class.Instance`.

p.s: The Instance to apply the tag to.
The tag string to apply to the instance.

kid.simple: Sticks a tag (a word) onto an object. If it already has that tag, nothing happens. Fires the tag's added signal.
kid.example:
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")
CollectionService:AddTag(workspace.Door, "Openable")
kid.gotcha: If a LocalScript adds a tag and the server later changes any tag on that object, the local tag disappears.

m.d:
This method creates a Collection, a live, query-based group of instances. Unlike tag-based methods such as GetTagged() which return a fixed array at the moment they are called, a Collection continuously tracks which instances match query and notifies you as instances enter and leave the result set.

The query string is a CSS-inspired selector that follows the same selector conventions used by QueryDescendants() and the StyleRule styling selectors. Filters stack conjunctively, combinators express hierarchy, and comma-separated selectors form a union:

  • ClassName — Instances of that class (uses IsA()), for example Part or Model.
  • #Name — Instances with a matching Name.
  • .Tag — Instances carrying a CollectionService tag.
  • [Property = value] — Instances whose property equals a value.
  • [$Attribute] or [$Attribute = value] — Instances that have an attribute, optionally matching a value.
  • A > B (direct child) and A >> B (any descendant) combinators.
  • :has(...) and :not(...) pseudoclasses.

The rightmost selector in a chain identifies the matched instance, so Folder > Part tracks the parts, not the folders.

local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")

-- Track every Part tagged "KillBrick" anywhere under Workspace
local killBricks: Collection = CollectionService:CreateCollection("Part.KillBrick")

-- When a part joins the collection, make it glow red
-- OnAdded fires once for each part already matching, then again for each new match
function killBricks.OnAdded(brick: Part)
    brick.Material = Enum.Material.Neon
    brick.Color = Color3.new(1, 0, 0)
end

-- Kill any humanoid that touches a matched part
function killBricks.OnTouched(brick: Part, otherPart: BasePart)
    local character: Instance? = otherPart.Parent
    local humanoid = character and character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if humanoid then
        humanoid.Health = 0
    end
end

-- Fires when a part stops matching (tag removed, reparented out, or destroyed)
function killBricks.OnRemoved(brick: Part)
    print("Deactivating", brick:GetFullName())
end

Notes

  • The collection remains active until you call Destroy() or its root is destroyed.
  • Lifecycle callbacks are queued rather than invoked synchronously, so a newly assigned OnAdded may fire on a later resumption point rather than during the assignment itself.
m.s: Creates a `Datatype.Collection` that tracks every instance matching a query.

p.s: A selector string describing which instances to match. See the description for the supported syntax.

The instance whose descendants are searched. Pass this to restrict the search to a subtree, such that instances outside that subtree never match and an instance is removed from the collection if it is reparented out of root. Defaults to Workspace when omitted.

r.s: A Collection that reactively tracks the instances matching query.

kid.simple: Makes a live group that always contains every object matching a search text (a query). Unlike `GetTagged`, which is a one-time snapshot, a Collection keeps updating: it calls your `OnAdded` function when something starts matching and `OnRemoved` when it stops. The query can be a class name (`Part`), a name (`#Door`), a tag (`.Lava`), or mixes like `Part.Lava`. By default it searches inside Workspace.
kid.example:
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")
-- every Part with the KillBrick tag, inside Workspace
local killBricks = CollectionService:CreateCollection("Part.KillBrick")

-- runs once for each matching part, now and in the future
function killBricks.OnAdded(brick)
    brick.Material = Enum.Material.Neon
    brick.Color = Color3.new(1, 0, 0)
end

-- runs when a matched part is touched
function killBricks.OnTouched(brick, otherPart)
    local humanoid = otherPart.Parent and otherPart.Parent:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if humanoid then
        humanoid.Health = 0
    end
end

-- runs when a part stops matching (tag removed or part deleted)
function killBricks.OnRemoved(brick)
    print("No longer a kill brick:", brick.Name)
end
kid.gotcha: The Collection keeps working until you call its `:Destroy()` method or the object it searches inside (the root) is destroyed.

This means calling GetAllTags() immediately after removing the last instance with a given tag will no longer include that tag.

Given a tag (string), this method returns a signal which fires under two conditions:

  • The tag is assigned to an instance within the DataModel using CollectionService:AddTag() or Instance:AddTag().

  • An instance with the given tag is added as a descendant of the DataModel, for example by setting Instance.Parent or similar.

Subsequent calls to this method with the same tag return the same signal object. Consider also calling GetTagged() to get a list of instances that already have a tag (and thus won't fire the event if they already are in the DataModel).

See also GetInstanceRemovedSignal() which returns an event that fires under similar conditions.

    print("A new coin appeared:", coin.Name)
end)

m.d:
Given a tag (string), this method returns a signal which fires under two conditions:

  • The tag is removed from an instance within the DataModel using CollectionService:RemoveTag() or Instance:RemoveTag().

  • An instance with the given tag is removed as a descendant of the DataModel, for example by un‑setting Instance.Parent or similar.

Subsequent calls to this method with the same tag return the same signal object. The signal is useful for cleaning up resources used by instances that once had tags, such as disconnecting connections.

See also GetInstanceAddedSignal() which returns an event that fires under similar conditions.
m.s: Returns a signal that fires when a given tag is removed from an instance.

p.s: The tag to watch for.

CollectionService:GetInstanceRemovedSignal("Coin"):Connect(function(coin)
    print("A coin was removed:", coin.Name)
end)

m.d:
This method returns an array of instances with a given tag which are descendants of the DataModel. Removing a tag using CollectionService:RemoveTag() or Instance:RemoveTag() ensures this method does not return them.

If you want to detect all instances with a tag, both present and future, use this method to iterate over instances while also making a connection to a signal returned by GetInstanceAddedSignal().

kid.simple: CollectionService lets you put name stickers, called tags, on objects. Then ONE script can find every object with a certain tag and give them all the same behavior. Instead of copying the same script into 50 lava bricks, you tag them all "Lava" and write one script that handles every Lava brick.
kid.analogy: Tags are like colored stickers in a classroom. Put a red sticker on every kid in the soccer club, and the coach can just say "everyone with a red sticker, come to the field" instead of calling 30 names.
whenToUse: Many objects should act the same way (lava, coins, doors, checkpoints)
Find all objects of one kind quickly, like every enemy spawn point
Run code automatically when a tagged object appears or disappears
Mark objects with a label, like "Breakable", and check for it later
kid.where: Server and client. Get it with game:GetService("CollectionService"). You can also add tags in Studio: select an object, then look in the Properties window under Tags.

terms.tag: A word you stick on an object, like "Lava" or "Coin". An object can have many tags. Tags are just text.
terms.instance: Any object in your game, like a Part, Model or Sound.
terms.DataModel: The whole game tree (everything you see in the Explorer window, starting at `game`).
terms.descendant: Anything inside something else, at any depth: its children, its children's children, and so on.
terms.replicate: To be copied from the server to every player's device automatically. Tags added on the server replicate to players.
terms.signal: An event object you can `:Connect` a function to. It runs your function every time it fires.
terms.query: A short search text describing which objects you want, like `Part.Lava` (Parts that have the Lava tag).
terms.Collection: A live group that keeps track of every object matching a query, adding and removing members automatically as things change.
terms.memory leak: When your game keeps holding on to stuff it no longer needs, which slowly makes it slower. Clean up connections when an object leaves.

examples.title: Every part tagged Lava hurts players
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (tag some parts "Lava" in the Properties window)
examples.code:
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")

local function makeLava(part)
    part.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
        -- otherPart might be a leg or arm; its Parent is the character
        local humanoid = otherPart.Parent:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
        if humanoid then
            humanoid.Health = 0
        end
    end)
end

-- set up all the Lava parts that already exist
for _, part in CollectionService:GetTagged("Lava") do
    makeLava(part)
end

-- and any Lava parts added later
CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal("Lava"):Connect(makeLava)
explain: `makeLava` gives one part the lava behavior.
`GetTagged("Lava")` returns a list of every object that has the Lava tag right now; we set each one up.
`GetInstanceAddedSignal("Lava")` fires whenever a new Lava-tagged object appears later, so those get set up too.
Now you can place 1 or 1,000 lava parts and you only ever wrote one script.

examples.title: Add and check tags from code
examples.code:
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")

local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Parent = workspace

CollectionService:AddTag(part, "Coin")           -- stick on a tag
print(CollectionService:HasTag(part, "Coin"))    -- true
print(CollectionService:GetTags(part))           -- {"Coin"}

CollectionService:RemoveTag(part, "Coin")        -- peel it off
print(CollectionService:HasTag(part, "Coin"))    -- false
explain: `AddTag` puts a tag on an object. `HasTag` checks for one. `GetTags` lists them all. `RemoveTag` takes one off.
Every object also has shortcut methods that do the same thing: `part:AddTag("Coin")`, `part:HasTag("Coin")`, `part:RemoveTag("Coin")`.

gotchas: `GetTagged` only finds objects that exist NOW. Also connect `GetInstanceAddedSignal` to catch ones added later.
Tags are case-sensitive: "Lava" and "lava" are different tags.
Tags added by a LocalScript only exist on that player's device, and they get wiped out if the server later changes tags on the same object.
Objects stored in ServerStorage are not inside Workspace, but they are still in the game, so `GetTagged` can still find them on the server.
When a tagged object is removed, disconnect any connections you made for it (use `GetInstanceRemovedSignal`) to avoid memory leaks.

class/CompositeValueCurve.d:
An animation curve that groups child FloatCurves which each animate a different component of a non-unary value. The CurveType property specifies the type of value to be animated and, depending on this value, differently named children are used to drive the animation of the components of the value.

As follows are the names of the child curves that drive the animation for each possible CompositeValueCurveType value for CurveType:

  • ColorRGB: { "R", "G", "B" }
  • ColorHSV: { "H", "S", "V" }
  • NumberRange: { "Min", "Max" }
  • Rect: { "MinX", "MaxX", "MinY", "MaxY" }
  • UDim: { "Scale", "Offset" }
  • UDim2: { "ScaleX", "OffsetX", "ScaleY", "OffsetY" }
  • Vector2: { "X", "Y"}
  • Vector3: { "X", "Y", "Z" }

The children that drive the animation can be accessed via the GetComponentCurves() method which returns an array of curves in the order specified above. The value of the curve at a given time in the animation may be sampled by the GetValueAtTime() method.
class/CompositeValueCurve.s: An animation curve that groups child `Class.FloatCurve|FloatCurves` which each animate a different component of a non-unary value.

m.d: This method returns the child curves with the given names for the CurveType of this CompositeValueCurve, in the order given by the list of child curves outlined at the top of this page. Any curve that does not exist prior to calling this method will be created and added as a child with the appropriate name. That new curve will be an empty FloatCurve.
m.s: Returns the child curves with the given names for the `Class.CompositeValueCurve.CurveType|CurveType` of this `Class.CompositeValueCurve`.

r.s: An array of the child FloatCurve instances that drive the components of the animated value, in the order listed at the top of this page. Any expected child curve that does not yet exist is created as an empty FloatCurve and included in the result.

m.d:
This method returns the sampled animated value at the passed time argument. The type of the returned value will match that specified by the CurveType property.

If any child curve is missing from the children of the curve, the corresponding value in the returned property will be 0. For example, if a curve has a CurveType of CompositeValueCurveType.ColorRGB but only one FloatCurve child named "G", then the returned FloatCurve will have values of 0 for "R" and "B", but the "G" value will be sampled from the child curve.

class/CompressorSoundEffect.d:
A CompressorSoundEffect is used to reduce the dynamic range of audio by moving the highs and lows of a signal closer together. It does this by lowering the volume of the highest parts of a source while at the same time raising the overall volume. This type of effect is useful when you have many sounds playing and you want to make sure the quieter ones are still audible. This effect can be applied to either an individual Sound or SoundGroup by parenting it to the desired instance.

A compressor has several properties which determine how it works. The Threshold is the audio level where the compressor will start to lower the volume. As soon as the source goes below the threshold, the compressor will stop lowering the volume.

The Attack determines how long it takes for the compressed effect to fully apply. After the threshold has been crossed the compressor will lower the volume over time until the desired ratio has been reached. It will take the time specified by Attack to reach this ratio.

The Release determines how long it takes for the compressor to remove its effect. After the volume of the source is under the threshold, the compressor will restore the volume back to the original over the time specified by Release.

Along with lowering the volume when the sound has passed the threshold, a compressor will also amplify the entire sound (after any threshold lowering has taken effect). This allows quieter sounds to be amplified while louder sounds can stay about the same. The GainMakeup determines how much the effect amplifies the sound.
class/CompressorSoundEffect.s: Adjusts the dynamic range of audio.

m.d: The time the effect takes to become active after its Threshold has been reached. Range is 0.1 to 1 (default 0.1), measured in seconds.
m.s: The time the effect takes to become active after its `Class.CompressorSoundEffect.Threshold|Threshold` has been reached.

m.d: The overall amplification applied to the effect's Sound or SoundGroup after attenuation of sounds above the threshold. Keep in mind this amplification will occur as long as the effect is active, regardless of whether the Threshold has been reached or not. Range is -30 to 30 (default 0), measured in dB.
m.s: The overall amplification applied to the effect's `Class.Sound` or `Class.SoundGroup` after attenuation of sounds above the threshold.

m.d: The ratio between the SideChain sound effect, and this sound effect.
m.s: The ratio between the `Class.CompressorSoundEffect.SideChain|SideChain` sound effect, and this sound effect.

m.d: The time the effect takes to become inactive after its sound is below the Threshold. Range is 0 to 5 (default 0.1), measured in seconds.
m.s: The time the effect takes to become inactive after its sound is below the `Class.CompressorSoundEffect.Threshold|Threshold`.

m.d: Applies a ducking effect to the compressor sound effect. The behavior of the sidechain depends on the Sound or SoundGroup linked to it.

m.d: Volume level at which point the compressor applies its effect. If the effect's Sound or SoundGroup is below the effect will not attenuate the sound, although the GainMakeup will still be applied. Range is -80 to 0 (default 0), measured in dB.

class/Configuration.d:
The Configuration object is a container object. It's designed to hold value objects to make their values more accessible to Tools or any model that uses Scripts.

How does the Configuration object work?

The Configuration object is just a container and does not automatically offer any additional functionality to a Folder.

Configurations should hold value objects (BrickColorValue, NumberValue, IntValue, ObjectValue, etc.). These value objects should be read by the Script or LocalScript associated with the configuration to determine constants such as damage, speed, or color.

For example, a script might include a damage variable:

local damage = 10

With a Configuration object, that code becomes:

local configuration = tool:FindFirstChildWhichIsA("Configuration", true)
damage = configuration:FindFirstChild("Damage").Value -- a NumberValue

The Configuration object is intended to be placed inside a BasePart in a Model or Tool. You can then edit its values in the Roblox Studio Properties window rather than having to update the code.

Typically, you would place the script within the same model or tool as the configuration, so you would have some confidence that the configuration existed and had certain values. If you fetch the configuration from an outside script, you should program more defensively, with if statements to check that the configuration and values exist and fallback values in the event that the Find() methods fail.

Why should I use the Configuration object?

Configurations can be convenient for tools and models that you want to use across a range of games or distribute in the Creator Store. The object makes it clear that all variables for the tool or model can be found in this one place, and other creators can make changes without having to modify your code.

For variables that you only want to use within a single game and that you want the flexibility to tune without publishing your experience, see Experience configs.

m.s: Indicates if the constraint is currently active in the world.

kid.simple: Read-only true/false that tells you if the constraint is really working right now. It is true only when the constraint and both of its parts are in workspace AND Enabled is true.
kid.example:
local rope = workspace.Ceiling.RopeConstraint
if not rope.Active then
	warn("Rope is not working - check its attachments!")
end
kid.gotcha: You cannot set Active yourself. To switch a constraint on or off, change Enabled instead.

m.d: The Attachment that is connected to Constraint.Attachment1
m.s: The `Class.Attachment` that is connected to `Class.Constraint.Attachment1`.

kid.simple: The first attachment (connection point) the constraint grabs. For pushing constraints like VectorForce, this is the one that gets pushed.
kid.example:
local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = workspace.Box

local force = Instance.new("VectorForce")
force.Attachment0 = attachment -- push the Box through this point
force.Parent = workspace.Box

m.d: The Attachment that is connected to Constraint.Attachment0
m.s: The `Class.Attachment` that is connected to `Class.Constraint.Attachment0`.

kid.simple: The second attachment the constraint connects to. For things like ropes and hinges it is the other end; for Align constraints it is the goal to move toward.
kid.example:
local rope = Instance.new("RopeConstraint")
rope.Attachment0 = workspace.Ceiling.Attachment
rope.Attachment1 = workspace.Ball.Attachment -- other end of the rope
rope.Parent = workspace.Ceiling

m.d: The color of the constraint.
m.s: The color of the constraint.

kid.simple: The color used when the constraint is drawn (for example the color of a visible rope or spring). It is a BrickColor.
kid.example:
local rope = workspace.Ceiling.RopeConstraint
rope.Visible = true
rope.Color = BrickColor.new("Bright red") -- red rope

m.d: Toggles whether or not the constraint is enabled.
m.s: Toggles whether or not the constraint is enabled.

kid.simple: The on/off switch. true means the constraint works; false means it is ignored, as if it was not there.
kid.example:
local spring = workspace.Car.SpringConstraint
spring.Enabled = false -- turn the spring off
task.wait(3)
spring.Enabled = true  -- and back on after 3 seconds

m.d: Toggles the constraint's visibility.
m.s: Toggles the constraint's visibility.

kid.simple: Whether the constraint is drawn so you can see it. Handy for ropes, rods and springs that players should see, or for debugging while you build.
kid.example:
local rope = workspace.Ceiling.RopeConstraint
rope.Visible = true -- show the rope as a line

Constraint is the family name for all the physics connectors in Roblox: hinges, ropes, springs, pushers and more. You never make a plain `Constraint` yourself; you make one of its children, like a `RopeConstraint` or a `VectorForce`. Every constraint shares a few settings: which two attachments it connects, whether it is turned on, and whether you can see it.
kid.analogy: Constraint is like the word 'tool' in a toolbox. You never pick up 'a tool'; you pick up a hammer or a screwdriver. But every tool has a handle, and every constraint has Attachment0, Attachment1 and Enabled.
whenToUse: Check `Active` to see if a constraint is really working right now
Turn any constraint on or off with `Enabled`
Hook any constraint up to parts using `Attachment0` and `Attachment1`
Write code that works on every kind of constraint with `obj:IsA("Constraint")`
kid.where: Works on the server and the client. You cannot create it directly; create a child class such as Instance.new("HingeConstraint"). It only works when it and its attachments are inside workspace.

terms.constraint: An invisible rule or connector that the physics engine follows, like 'these two parts must stay stuck together' or 'push this part upward'.
terms.physics engine: The part of Roblox that moves unanchored parts around every frame: makes them fall, bounce, slide and spin.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.anchored: An anchored part is frozen in place. Physics and constraint forces cannot move it. Set `part.Anchored = false` if you want a constraint to move it.
terms.property: A setting on an object, like `Color` or `Enabled`, that you can read or change.
terms.deprecated: Old and replaced by something better. It may still work, but you should not use it in new games.
terms.Instance.new: The function that creates a brand-new object from a script, like Instance.new("Attachment").
terms.IsA: A check that asks 'is this object this kind of thing (or a child kind of it)?'. A RopeConstraint IsA Constraint, so `rope:IsA("Constraint")` is true.
terms.BrickColor: Roblox's list of named colors, like BrickColor.new("Bright red").

examples.title: Turn off every constraint in a model
examples.place: Script inside a Model in Workspace
examples.code:
local model = script.Parent

-- Look at everything inside the model, even things nested deep inside
for _, thing in model:GetDescendants() do
	-- Is it any kind of constraint? (rope, hinge, spring...)
	if thing:IsA("Constraint") then
		thing.Enabled = false -- switch it off
	end
end
explain: `script.Parent` is the model this script sits inside.
`GetDescendants()` gives a list of every object inside the model, including things inside things.
`IsA("Constraint")` is true for every constraint type, so this one check catches ropes, hinges, springs and all the others.
Setting `Enabled = false` switches the constraint off, so the parts are no longer held or pushed by it.

examples.title: Hook a rope between two parts
examples.code:
-- Two parts already in the workspace
local top = workspace:WaitForChild("Ceiling")   -- anchored part
local ball = workspace:WaitForChild("Ball")     -- unanchored part

-- Every constraint grabs parts through attachments
local a0 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a0.Parent = top
local a1 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a1.Parent = ball

local rope = Instance.new("RopeConstraint")
rope.Attachment0 = a0
rope.Attachment1 = a1
rope.Length = 8          -- 8 studs long
rope.Visible = true      -- draw it so players can see it
rope.Parent = top

task.wait(1)
print("Is the rope working?", rope.Active)
explain: Constraints never connect parts directly. They connect attachments, and each attachment lives inside a part.
We make one attachment in the ceiling and one in the ball.
`Attachment0` and `Attachment1` are the two ends of the rope.
`Active` becomes true once the rope and both parts are in the workspace and Enabled is on.

gotchas: A constraint does nothing until BOTH Attachment0 and Attachment1 are set (except a few that only need Attachment0, like VectorForce and Torque).
Forces cannot move anchored parts. If nothing happens, check that the part you want to move has Anchored = false.
Constraints only work inside workspace. One sitting in ReplicatedStorage or ServerStorage does nothing.

class/ContentProvider.d:
Service that loads content (assets) into a game.

Roblox servers stream all assets to the client at runtime: objects in the Workspace, mesh assets, texture assets, etc. Assets such as mesh visual data, textures, decals, and sounds are streamed in as required, regardless of whether Streaming is enabled.

In some cases, this behavior is undesirable, as it can lead to a delay before the content loads into the experience.

ContentProvider lets you preload assets into an experience using the ContentProvider:PreloadAsync() method. You might want to display a loading screen, preload critical assets, and only then allow the player into the experience.

Best Practices for Preloading

  • Only preload essential assets, not the entire Workspace. You might get occasional pop-in, but it decreases load times and generally doesn't disrupt the player experience. Assets that are good candidates for preloading include those required for the loading screen, the UI, or the starting area.
  • Let players skip the loading screen, or automatically skip it after a certain amount of time.
class/ContentProvider.s: Service that is used to load content, or assets, into a game.

m.d:
Used by the ContentProvider to download assets from the Roblox website.

This URL points to a Roblox hosted website from which assets are downloaded and is pulled from the AppSettings.xml file, located in the version-hash folder.

It is possible to overwrite this property using the ContentProvider:SetBaseUrl() function in the command bar; however, this is not recommended and may cause asset loading issues.
m.s: Used by the `Class.ContentProvider` to download assets from the Roblox website.

m.d:
Gives the number of items in the ContentProvider request queue that need to be downloaded.

Items are added to the client's request queue when an asset is used for the first time or ContentProvider:PreloadAsync() is called.

Developers are advised not to use RequestQueueSize to create loading bars. This is because the queue size can both increase and decrease over time as new assets are added and downloaded. Developers looking to display loading progress should load assets one at a time (see example below).
m.s: Gives the number of items in the `Class.ContentProvider` request queue that need to be downloaded.

m.d: Gets the current AssetFetchStatus of the contentId provided. Use GetAssetFetchStatusChangedSignal() to listen for changes to this value.
m.s: Gets the current `Enum.AssetFetchStatus` of the `contentId` provided.

p.s: The ID of the content to fetch the status for.

r.s: The AssetFetchStatus of the content.

m.d: A signal that fires when the AssetFetchStatus of the provided content changes. Connect to this signal by using a callback with one argument of type AssetFetchStatus. This is particularly useful for assets that might update themselves automatically like the thumbnail of a user when they change clothes.
m.s: A signal that fires when the `Enum.AssetFetchStatus` of the provided content changes.

p.s: The ID of the content to monitor for fetch status changes.

r.s: An RBXScriptSignal that fires when the AssetFetchStatus of the given content changes.

m.d:
Returns an array containing every asset ID that currently has an encryption key registered on this ContentProvider, whether the key was registered directly through RegisterEncryptedAsset() or through RegisterSessionEncryptedAsset().

The default key set through RegisterDefaultEncryptionKey() is not included, because it isn't associated with any specific asset.
m.s: Returns an array of the asset IDs that currently have a registered encryption key.

r.s: An array of the asset IDs that currently have an encryption key registered on this ContentProvider.

m.d: Usually, content is loaded only when it starts being used. That explains why it often takes a moment for an image to appear in a GuiObject, or a Mesh|mesh to appear in a part, or why a sound doesn't play for the first time. All because the asset has not yet finished loading. Preload is used to load this content beforehand, so that it works instantly.
m.s: Queues an asset to be downloaded by the `Class.ContentProvider`.

p.s: The content URL of the asset to preload.

m.dep: This item has been superseded by ContentProvider:PreloadAsync() which should be used in all new work.

m.d:
Yields until all of the assets associated with the given Instances have loaded. This can be used to pause a script and not use content until it is certain that the content has been loaded into the experience.

When called, the engine identifies links to content for each item in the list. For any of the Instances which have properties that define links to content, such as a Decal or a Sound, the engine attempts to load these assets from Roblox. For each requested asset, the callback function runs, indicating the asset's final AssetFetchStatus.

If any of the assets fail to load, an error message appears in the output. The method itself will not error and it will continue executing until it has processed each requested instance.

Limitations

SurfaceAppearance and MaterialVariant are not supported by PreloadAsync() because these objects rely on processed texture pack assets rather than directly loading individual textures. Calling it on a SurfaceAppearance instance will not do anything, but the associated textures will still be streamed in during runtime.

If PreloadAsync is called on Instances that are not currently visible, such as a Decal or an ImageLabel, the Engine will download and store textures used by those Instances in its disk cache. Because the Instances are not visible in these cases, the Engine may reduce memory consumption by unloading the textures after preloading them.
m.s: Yields until all of the assets associated with the given `Class.Instance|Instances` have loaded.

p.s: An array of instances to load.
The function called when each asset request completes. Returns the content string and the asset's final AssetFetchStatus.

m.d: Sets a fallback encryption key that the ContentProvider uses to decrypt any encrypted asset that isn't matched by a key registered for a specific asset through RegisterEncryptedAsset(). When an asset is fetched, the engine first looks for a key registered for that asset's ID; if none exists, it falls back to this default key.
m.s: Registers a fallback encryption key used to decrypt any encrypted asset that doesn't have its own key registered.

p.s: The key to use as the default for decrypting encrypted assets.

m.d: Decrypts sessionKey using the session's cryptographic context and then registers the decrypted result as the default encryption key, exactly as RegisterDefaultEncryptionKey() does. Use this variant when the key is delivered to the client in session-encrypted form rather than as plaintext.
m.s: Decrypts the provided session key and registers the result as the default encryption key.

p.s: The session-encrypted key to decrypt and register as the default encryption key.

m.d: Associates encryptionKey with the given assetId so that, when the ContentProvider fetches that asset, it uses the key to decrypt the downloaded file. A key registered for a specific asset takes precedence over the default key set through RegisterDefaultEncryptionKey(). The method throws an error if assetId isn't a valid asset ID.
m.s: Registers an encryption key used to decrypt a specific encrypted asset.

p.s: The asset to associate the encryption key with.
The key used to decrypt the specified asset.

m.d: Decrypts sessionKey using the session's cryptographic context and then registers the decrypted result as the encryption key for contentId, exactly as RegisterEncryptedAsset() does. Use this variant when the per-asset key is delivered to the client in session-encrypted form rather than as plaintext.
m.s: Decrypts the provided session key and registers it as the encryption key for a specific asset.

p.s: The asset to associate the decrypted key with.
The session-encrypted key to decrypt and register for the specified asset.

m.d: Removes the default encryption key registered through RegisterDefaultEncryptionKey(), so that assets without a specifically registered key are no longer decrypted with a fallback key. Keys registered for individual assets through RegisterEncryptedAsset() are unaffected.
m.s: Clears the default encryption key previously set on the `Class.ContentProvider`.

m.d: Removes the encryption key associated with assetId by RegisterEncryptedAsset(), so the asset is no longer decrypted with that key. If no key is registered for the asset, the call has no effect.
m.s: Removes the encryption key registered for a specific asset.

p.s: The asset whose registered encryption key should be removed.

m.d: Fires when an asset requested through the ContentProvider fails to be fetched, passing the content ID of the asset that failed.
m.s: Fires when the `Class.ContentProvider` fails to fetch an asset, passing the asset's ID.

p.s: The content ID of the asset that failed to load.

class/ContextActionService.d:
Allows an experience to bind user input to contextual actions, or actions that are only enabled under some condition or period of time. For example, allowing a player to open a door only while close by. In code, an action is simply a string (the name of the action) used by the service to differentiate between unique actions. The action string is provided to BindAction and UnbindAction, among other member functions. If two actions are bound to the same input, the most recently bound will take priority. When the most recent action is unbound, the one bound before that takes control again. Since this service deals with user input, you can only use it in client-side LocalScripts.

Context and Action

A context is simply a condition during which a player may perform some action. Some examples include holding a Tool, being seated in a car or standing near a door. Whatever the case may be, it is up to your LocalScripts to call BindAction when the context is entered and UnbindAction when the context is left.

An action is simply some input that can be performed by the player while in that context. Such an action could open/close some menu, trigger a secondary tool action or send a request to the server using RemoteFunction:InvokeServer(). An action is identified by a unique string as the first parameter of both BindAction and UnbindAction. The string can be anything, but it should reflect the action being performed, not the input being used. For example, don't use "KeyH" as an action name - use "CarHorn" instead. It is best to define your actions as a constant at the top of your script since you will use it in at least three different places in your code.

Binding Actions Contextually

It's better to use ContextActionService's BindAction than UserInputService.InputBegan for most cases. For UserInputService.InputBegan, your connected function would have to check if the player is in the context of the action being performed. In most cases, this is harder than just calling a function when a context is entered/ left. For example, if you want to have the H key trigger a car horn sound while the player is sitting in it, the player might type "hello" in chat or otherwise use the H key for something else. It is harder to determine if something else is using the H key (like chat) - the car might honk when the player didn't mean to. If you instead use BindAction and UnbindAction when the player enters/leaves the car, ContextActionService will make sure that H key presses trigger the honk action only when it is the most recently bound action. If something else (like chat) takes control, you won't have to worry about checking that.

Inspecting Bound Actions

To see a list of actions and their bound inputs, you can inspect the "Action Bindings" tab in the Developer Console (F9 while in game). This shows all bindings, including those bound by Roblox core scripts and default camera/control scripts too. This is useful for debugging if your actions are being bound/unbound at the correct times, or if some other action is stealing input from your actions. For example, if you are attempting to bind WASD, it may be the case that default character movement scripts are binding over those same keys. Similarly, the camera control script can steal right-click input if the script runs after yours.

Keyboardless Input

This service is especially useful for supporting gamepad and touch input. For gamepad input, you might choose to bind the B button to an action that returns the user to the previous menu when they enter another menu. For touch, on-screen touch buttons can be used in place of key presses: these buttons display only while the action is bound, and the position, text and/or images of these buttons can be configured through this service. They're somewhat limited in the amount of customization provided by this service; it's usually a better idea to make your own on-screen buttons using ImageButton or TextButton.
class/ContextActionService.s: A service used to bind user input to contextual actions.

m.d:
Bind an action to user input given an action handling function. Upon a matching input being performed, the action handler function will be called with the arguments listed below. Valid input enum items include those within the following: KeyCode, UserInputType or PlayerActions . Call this function when a player enters the context in which an action can be performed. When the player leaves the context, call UnbindAction() with the same actionName.

The code sample below shows how a Sound can be played while a key (H), game pad button, or touch screen button is pressed.

local ContextActionService = game:GetService("ContextActionService")

-- A car horn sound
local honkSound = Instance.new("Sound", workspace)
honkSound.Looped = true
honkSound.SoundId = "rbxassetid://9120386436"

local function handleAction(actionName, inputState, inputObject)
    if actionName == "HonkHorn" then
        if inputState == Enum.UserInputState.Begin then
            honkSound:Play()
        else
            honkSound:Pause()
        end
    end
end

-- When the player sits in the vehicle:
ContextActionService:BindAction("HonkHorn", handleAction, true, Enum.KeyCode.H, Enum.KeyCode.ButtonY)

-- When the player gets out:
ContextActionService:UnbindAction("HonkHorn")

Action Handler Parameters

The action handler functions are called with the following parameters:

# Type Description
1 string The same string that was originally passed to Class.ContextActionService:BindAction()|BindAction(). This allows one function to handle multiple actions at once, if necessary.
2 Enum.UserInputState The state of the input. Enum.UserInputState|Cancel is sent if some input was in progress and another action bound over that in-progress input, or if the in-progress bound action was unbound through Class.ContextActionService:UnbindAction()|UnbindAction().
3 InputObject An object that contains information about the input (varies based on Enum.UserInputType). The Class.InputObject sometimes won't match the inputs the action was bound to: when the Enum.UserInputState|Cancel state is sent, this object will be Enum.KeyCode.Unknown and Enum.UserInputType.None.

Action Bindings Stack

Action bindings behave like a stack: if two actions are bound to the same user input, the most recently bound action handler will be used. If an action handler returns ContextActionResult.Pass, the next most recently bound action handler will be called, and so on until a handler sinks the input (by returning nil or ContextActionResult.Sink). When UnbindAction is called, the action handler is removed from the stack. This stack behavior can be overridden using BindActionAtPriority, where an additional priority parameter after createTouchButton may override the order in which actions are bound (higher before lower).

Touch Buttons

In addition to input types, this function's third parameter controls whether a button is created for TouchEnabled devices. Upon the first touch button's creation, a ScreenGui named "ContextActionGui" is added to the PlayerGui. Inside the ScreenGui is a Frame called "ContextButtonFrame" is added. It is in this frame in which ImageButtons for bound actions are parented; you can use GetButton() to retrieve such buttons for customization. A maximum of 7 touch buttons can be created through BindAction().
m.s: Bind user input to an action given an action handling function.

p.s: A string representing the action being performed (e.g. "HonkHorn" or "OpenDoor").
The action-handling function, called with the following parameters when the bound inputs are triggered: string (actionName), UserInputState and an InputObject.
Whether a GUI button should be created for the action on touch input devices.
Any number of KeyCode or UserInputType representing the inputs to bind to the action.

kid.simple: Connects an action name to one or more keys or buttons. When one is pressed or released, your handler function runs with (actionName, inputState, inputObject). The third value, true or false, says whether to make an on-screen button for touch devices. The newest binding on a key wins.
kid.example:
local ContextActionService = game:GetService("ContextActionService")
local function onReload(actionName, inputState, inputObject)
    if inputState == Enum.UserInputState.Begin then
        print("Reloading!")
    end
end
ContextActionService:BindAction("Reload", onReload, true, Enum.KeyCode.R, Enum.KeyCode.ButtonX)
kid.gotcha: Remember to `UnbindAction` when the situation is over, or the key keeps doing the action.

m.d: BindActionAtPriority behaves like BindAction but also allows a priority to be assigned to the bound action. If multiple actions are bound to the same input, the higher priority function is called regardless of the order in which the actions were bound. In other words, this function overrides the normal "stack" behavior of BindAction.
m.s: Behaves like `Class.ContextActionService:BindAction()|BindAction` but also allows a priority to be assigned to the bound action for overlapping input types (higher before lower).

p.s: A string representing the action being performed (e.g. "HonkHorn" or "OpenDoor").
The action-handling function, called with the following parameters when the bound inputs are triggered: string (actionName), UserInputState and an InputObject.
Whether a GUI button should be created for the action on touch input devices.
The priority level at which the action should be bound (higher considered before lower).
Any number of Enum.KeyCode or Enum.UserInputType representing the inputs to bind to the action.

kid.simple: Like `BindAction`, but you also give a priority number. When two actions share a key, the one with the HIGHER priority runs first, no matter which was bound last.
kid.example:
local ContextActionService = game:GetService("ContextActionService")
local function onUse(actionName, inputState, inputObject)
    if inputState == Enum.UserInputState.Begin then
        print("Use (high priority)")
    end
end
-- 4th value is the priority: higher goes first
ContextActionService:BindActionAtPriority("Use", onUse, false, 3000, Enum.KeyCode.E)

m.d:
This function binds functionToBind to input events such as key presses, mouse movement, or controller input. The specific input types the engine listens for are listed as parameters of BindAction. Whenever a player uses any of these input types, the Roblox Engine calls "functionToBind". BindAction sets the priorityLevel via ContextActionPriority to Default.Value, which is 2000. Use ContextActionService:GetButton() to control the priority of bound events.

In addition to input types, BindAction has a createTouchButton parameter. When this is set to true it creates an ImageButton on any device with a touchscreen. A ScreenGui is also created to put the context buttons into named ContextActionGui and is parented to PlayerGui. The created ImageButton is parented to this ContextActionGui. GetButton can be used to retrieve the button that was created.

If an input has more than one function bound to it, each function will be placed on a stack. A stack obeys the principle of last in first out. So the first object placed on the stack will be on the top. The next object placed on the stack becomes the top and the previous object moves one position down (like a stack of books). When the input is triggered, the function at the top of the stack is called. If the function returns ContextActionResult.Pass this will continue down the stack. To remove a function from being called by all input that it was bound by use ContextActionService:UnbindAction().

BindAction allows control over whether or not a bound action should be processed by other actions on the stack using ContextActionResult. If ContextActionResult.Pass is returned in the callback function, every action below it in the stack (last function called gets executed first) will get a chance to process it. Anything other than Pass will be treated as ContextActionResult.Sink, including nil. It will also sink if the callback is yielded.
m.s: Binds _functionToBind_ to input events such as key presses, mouse movement, or controller input.
m.dep: This item has been superseded by ContextActionService:BindAction() which should be used in all new work.

kid.simple: Old — use `ContextActionService:BindAction` instead.

m.d:
Bind a KeyCode that can be used with a UserInputType to activate ClickDetector events, Tools, and GuiButtons. When the given key/button is pressed, it fires the Mouse.Button1Down event on the mouse sent to Tool.Equipped. This in turn fires the Tool.Activated event if Tool.ManualActivationOnly is not set to true. For gamepad input, this function is called by the default control scripts in order to bind the ButtonR2 KeyCode.

Note that the UserInputType specified must be Keyboard or Gamepad1 through Gamepad8 in order to be valid.
m.s: Bind a `Enum.KeyCode` with a specific `Enum.UserInputType` to trigger `Class.Tool.Activation` and `Class.ClickDetector` events.

p.s: Must be Keyboard or Gamepad1 through Gamepad8.
Any number of KeyCode values that trigger Tool activation for the specified UserInputType.

kid.simple: Picks a keyboard key or controller button that "activates" things like Tools, ClickDetectors and GUI buttons, as if the player clicked. Roblox already uses this to make the R2 trigger fire tools on controllers.
kid.example:
local ContextActionService = game:GetService("ContextActionService")
-- make the F key use the equipped tool, like a click
ContextActionService:BindActivate(Enum.UserInputType.Keyboard, Enum.KeyCode.F)
kid.gotcha: The input type must be `Keyboard` or one of `Gamepad1` to `Gamepad8`.

m.d: GetAllBoundActioninfo returns a table which maps all actions' names (those originally passed to BindAction) to a table returned by GetBoundActionInfo when called with the action name itself. Using this function, you can inspect all presently bound actions. This is useful when debugging their priority levels or stack orders.
m.s: Get a table of information about all bound actions (key is the name passed to `Class.ContextActionService:BindAction()|BindAction`, value is a table from `Class.ContextActionService:GetBoundActionInfo()|GetBoundActionInfo` when called with the key).

r.s: A dictionary mapping each bound action name to its info table.

kid.simple: Gives a table of every bound action and its details (like priority and order). Handy for figuring out why a key is not doing what you expect.
kid.example:
local ContextActionService = game:GetService("ContextActionService")
for actionName, info in ContextActionService:GetAllBoundActionInfo() do
    print(actionName, info.priorityLevel, info.stackOrder)
end

m.d:
GetBoundActionInfo returns a table with the following keys describing a bound action given its name. To get the same information for all actions at once, use GetAllBoundActionInfo.

Name Type Description
stackOrder number Describes the index of the action on the stack (increasing)
priorityLevel* number Describes the Class.ContextActionService:BindActionAtPriority()|priority level of the action
createTouchButton bool Describes whether a touch button should be created on Class.UserInputService.TouchEnabled|TouchEnabled devices
inputTypes table The input types passed to Class.ContextActionService:BindAction()|BindAction for which this action will trigger
description† string The description of action set by Class.ContextActionService:SetDescription()|SetDescription
title† string The title of the action set by Class.ContextActionService:SetTitle()|SetTitle
image† string The image of the action's touch button set by Class.ContextActionService:SetImage()|SetImage

* Priority level will still be included even if BindActionAtPriority wasn't used - by default it will be 2000.

† Indicates that this field will be nil if the associated method was not called for the given action.
m.s: Get a table of information about a bound action given its name originally passed to `Class.ContextActionService:BindAction()|BindAction`.

p.s: The name of the action originally passed to BindAction.

kid.simple: ContextActionService connects a player's buttons to an action in your game, but only while it makes sense. For example, the H key honks the horn only while you sit in a car. You give the action a name, list the keys or buttons, and it calls your function when they are pressed. It can even make an on-screen button for phone players automatically.
kid.analogy: It is like a TV remote whose buttons change job depending on which app is open. In the car app, the H button honks. Leave the car, and you unplug that job so H does nothing (or goes back to its old job).
whenToUse: A key that should only work in certain situations, like near a door, in a car, or holding a tool
One action that works on keyboard, controller and phone at the same time
Automatically making a touch button for phone and tablet players
Temporarily taking over a key, then giving it back when you are done
kid.where: Client only. Use it in a LocalScript (for example in StarterPlayerScripts or inside a Tool) with game:GetService("ContextActionService").

terms.context: A situation where an action is allowed, like sitting in a car or standing near a door.
terms.action: Something the player can do in that situation, identified by a name you choose, like "HonkHorn" or "OpenDoor".
terms.bind: To connect an action to some keys or buttons so your function runs when they are pressed.
terms.unbind: To disconnect it again, so the keys stop doing that action.
terms.handler (action handler): Your function that runs when the action's input happens. It receives the action name, the input state, and the InputObject.
terms.UserInputState: What stage the input is in: `Begin` (just pressed), `Change` (moving, like a joystick), `End` (released) or `Cancel` (interrupted, for example the action was unbound while the key was held).
terms.InputObject: A package of information about the input, like which key (`KeyCode`) and what type (`UserInputType`).
terms.stack: A pile where the newest thing goes on top. If two actions use the same key, the one bound most recently is on top and gets the press first.
terms.sink / pass: When your handler is done with a press, it can return `Enum.ContextActionResult.Sink` (eat it, nobody else gets it; this is also what happens if you return nothing) or `Enum.ContextActionResult.Pass` (let the next action on the stack have it too).
terms.priority: A number for ordering. With `BindActionAtPriority`, higher numbers get the input first.
terms.touch button: An on-screen button for phone and tablet players.
terms.UDim2: A GUI position or size made of a scale part (a fraction of the screen, like 0.5 for half) and an offset part (an exact number of pixels).

examples.title: Honk a horn with H, controller Y, or a phone button
examples.code:
local ContextActionService = game:GetService("ContextActionService")

local ACTION_HONK = "HonkHorn"

local honk = Instance.new("Sound")
honk.SoundId = "rbxassetid://9120386436" -- a car horn sound
honk.Looped = true
honk.Parent = workspace

local function handleAction(actionName, inputState, inputObject)
    if actionName == ACTION_HONK then
        if inputState == Enum.UserInputState.Begin then
            honk:Play()   -- button pressed: start honking
        else
            honk:Stop()   -- released (or cancelled): stop
        end
    end
    return Enum.ContextActionResult.Sink -- we used this input
end

-- when the player gets in the car (here: right away, for testing)
ContextActionService:BindAction(ACTION_HONK, handleAction, true, Enum.KeyCode.H, Enum.KeyCode.ButtonY)
ContextActionService:SetTitle(ACTION_HONK, "Honk") -- text on the phone button

-- when the player gets out of the car, call:
-- ContextActionService:UnbindAction(ACTION_HONK)
explain: We store the action name in a variable at the top, because we use it in several places.
`BindAction` takes: the action name, our handler function, `true` to make a phone button, and then any keys or buttons (H on the keyboard, Y on a controller).
Our handler gets the input state: `Begin` when pressed and `End` when released, so the horn plays only while held.
`SetTitle` puts the word "Honk" on the phone button.
Calling `UnbindAction` when they leave the car makes H stop honking.

gotchas: Only works in LocalScripts. Changes for everyone need a RemoteEvent to the server.
Your handler runs for BOTH press and release (and sometimes Cancel). Check `inputState` or your action will happen twice.
Returning nothing counts as Sink, which blocks other actions on the same key. Return `Enum.ContextActionResult.Pass` if you want other things (like default movement) to still get the key.
Binding a key the game already uses (like W or Space) takes it over until you unbind it, so the player may not be able to walk or jump.
Name actions after what they do ("OpenDoor"), not the key ("KeyE").
Only up to 7 touch buttons can be created this way.

class/ControllerBase.d: ControllerBase is the abstract base class for the controllers that a ControllerManager uses to move its assigned character: GroundController, AirController, SwimController, and ClimbController. Each controller is parented to a ControllerManager and supplies the movement and balance behavior for one locomotion state, and the manager activates one controller at a time. This class isn't created directly; instead create one of its derived controllers. It defines the balance and movement properties shared by all of them.
class/ControllerBase.s: Abstract base class for the controllers that a `Class.ControllerManager` uses to move its character.

m.d: Indicates whether this controller is the one currently driving its parent ControllerManager. The manager activates the controller referenced by its ControllerManager.ActiveController property and sets that controller's Active to true; when the controller is no longer the active one, it is deactivated and Active returns to false. This property is read-only and defaults to false.
m.s: Whether this controller is currently the active controller of its `Class.ControllerManager`.

m.d: Controls how the controller keeps its character oriented while active. When false (the default), the balance constraint is compliant and corrects orientation with a spring-damper response tuned by the controller's balance properties, such as its balance torque and balance speed. When true, the constraint instead holds the target orientation rigidly, and those balance-tuning properties no longer apply. Defaults to false.
m.s: Whether the controller holds its balance orientation rigidly instead of with a spring response.

m.d: The value multiplied by the ControllerManager.BaseMoveSpeed to determine the final desired linear velocity while this controller is active.
m.s: The value multiplied by the `Class.ControllerManager.BaseMoveSpeed`.

class/ControllerManager.d: The ControllerManager instance manages simulated motion control for its assigned ControllerManager.RootPart. It can be used to build a physics-based character controller.

If the ControllerBase cannot be activated for whatever reason, such as being outside of the character's WorldRoot or no Part being found to use as the floor for a GroundController, it will remain set and the ControllerManager will attempt to activate it in the next frame. This property can be set to nil to disable the physics controller.
m.s: The `Class.ControllerBase` that is set to be activated on the character.

m.s: The base angular turning speed used by all controllers.

A ClimbController will use the ControllerPartSensor.HitPart, ControllerPartSensor.HitFrame, and ControllerPartSensor.HitNormal for climb movement computations. Typically a ControllerPartSensor set to SensorMode.Ladder is used here. Otherwise, you can override the sensor's outputs to direct what sensor data you want the ClimbController to use.

A GroundController will use the ControllerPartSensor.HitPart, ControllerPartSensor.HitFrame, and ControllerPartSensor.HitNormal for ground movement computations. m.s: A reference to the sensor data used while a `Class.GroundController` is active.

For example, a GroundController applies levitation and balancing forces along this direction, while an AirController and SwimController align the character to it. A ControllerManager reads its ControllerManager.GroundSensor and ControllerManager.ClimbSensor, both of which are ControllerSensors, to determine how its ControllerManager.RootPart interacts with the world.

class/CurveAnimation.d:
CurveAnimation is a subtype of AnimationClip consumed by Roblox's animation system. It stores animation data for each animated channel in a rig as a separate, individual curve. For example, CurveAnimation stores the position channel for an articulated joint as a Vector3Curve, and it might store the rotation channel as a EulerRotationCurve or RotationCurve.

Structure

CurveAnimation stores curves in a hierarchical manner, matching the hierarchy of the structure of Motor6Ds or Bones in the animated model. Under each CurveAnimation instance lies a hierarchy of Folder instances representing animated joints in the model. Under each such folder instance, several possible instances may exist. An instance named Position of type Vector3Curve can drive the local translation of the Motor6D or Bone on the animated model, while an instance named Rotation of type EulerRotationCurve or RotationCurve can drive the local rotation of the Motor6D or Bone on the animated model.

Partial matching of hierarchy

You can match partial hierarchies to a model when playing a CurveAnimation in Roblox's animation system. This means that not all joints need to be present in the hierarchy for the existing joints to apply properly. Furthermore, you can match hierarchies in a "relative" manner. For example, the first child Folder instance root can be UpperTorso and the animation system matches that to any existing sub-hierarchies in the model.

Animating miscellaneous channels

CurveAnimation can also animate other numerical values in a model. For example, you can animate FACS controls for facial animations by creating a Folder under the CurveAnimation instance named after an existing FaceControls instance in the model. Then, to animate individual facial controllers, you can store individual FloatCurve instances named after the animated FaceControls property.

Usage when making animations

As with other AnimationClip types such as KeyframeSequence, you must first upload CurveAnimation instances to Roblox before playing them. If you want to preview an animation before uploading it to Roblox, you can generate a temporary ID using AnimationClipProvider:RegisterAnimationClip(); this generates a hash ID that you can use for localized animation testing.

If you want to download the CurveAnimation corresponding to an existing uploaded animation using Luau scripts, use AnimationClipProvider:GetAnimationClipAsync().

class/CylinderMesh.d:
The CylinderMesh object applies a 'cylinder' mesh to the BasePart it is parented to.

What does a CylinderMesh do?

A CylinderMesh gives the BasePart it was applied to a cylinder shaped mesh.

The mesh applied gives the same appearance as that due to the SpecialMesh.MeshType of a SpecialMesh being set to 'Cylinder' or Part.Shape being set to 'Cylinder'. However, unlike those two cases, it is orientated so that the height of the cylinder is along the BasePart Y axis.

The dimensions of the mesh scale relative to the BasePart.Size of the BasePart. This scale is uniformly along the BasePart Y axis and maintaining a 1:1 ratio for the part's X and Z axis, using the lowest value. This means the BasePart can be resized normally, but the cross section of the cylinder will always remain a circle and cannot be stretched or compressed.

Note as the CylinderMesh object does not include a texture the DataModelMesh.VertexColor property does not do anything.

Why use a CylinderMesh?

The advantage of using a mesh over setting the Part.Shape property of a part to 'Cylinder' is that the DataModelMesh.Scale and DataModelMesh.Offset properties are exposed. These allow the position and dimensions of the mesh that is displayed to be changed without changing the BasePart.Position or BasePart.Size of the Part the mesh is parented to.

The key difference between a CylinderMesh or a SpecialMesh with SpecialMesh.MeshType set to 'Cylinder' is the orientation of the cylinder mesh. With a CylinderMesh, the height of the cylinder is aligned with the height (Y axis) of the part. With a SpecialMesh (or Part with Part.Shape set to 'Cylinder'), the height of the cylinder is aligned with the X axis.

class/CylindricalConstraint.d:
A CylindricalConstraint allows its attachments to slide along one axis and rotate about another axis. It can be thought of like a combination of a PrismaticConstraint and a HingeConstraint. The sliding axis is determined by the X axis of the constraint's Attachment0. The rotation axis is centered at the constraint's Attachment1 and is angled off of the sliding constraint by the constraint's InclinationAngle.

This constraint, along with a SpringConstraint, is ideal for building vehicle suspension.

Note that if this constraint attaches one part (A) to another part (B) that is anchored or connected to an anchored part (Z), part A will not be locally simulated when interacting with a player.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Angular Power

If a cylindrical's AngularActuatorType is set to Motor, it attempts to rotate the attachments with the goal of reaching its AngularVelocity. You can further control this rotation through both MotorMaxAngularAcceleration and MotorMaxTorque. If a cylindrical's AngularActuatorType is set to Servo, it attempts to rotate to an angle specified by TargetAngle. This rotation is controlled by AngularSpeed, AngularResponsiveness, and ServoMaxTorque.

Linear Power

If a cylindrical's ActuatorType is set to Motor, it attempts to translate the attachments with the goal of reaching Velocity. You can further control this translation through both MotorMaxAcceleration and MotorMaxForce. If a cylindrical's ActuatorType is set to Servo, it attempts to translate the attachments to a set separation specified by TargetPosition. This translation is controlled by Speed, LinearResponsiveness, and ServoMaxForce.

Limits

You can set limits to restrict both the sliding range and rotation of a cylindrical constraint. Enabling the LimitsEnabled property exposes the LowerLimit and UpperLimit values, as well as Restitution which defines the elasticity of the attachments when they reach either limit. Enabling the AngularLimitsEnabled property exposes the LowerAngle and UpperAngle limits, as well as AngularRestitution which defines the elasticity of the attachments when they reach either limit.

Inclination Angle

InclinationAngle defines the direction of the rotation axis as an angle from the X axis in the XY plane of Attachment0, from -180 to 180. This lets you tilt the rotating element without changing the sliding axis.

terms.constraint: An invisible rule or connector that the physics engine follows, like 'these two parts must stay stuck together' or 'push this part upward'.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.axis: An imaginary line something turns around or slides along. An attachment's X axis is its main arrow.
terms.torque: A twisting push that makes things spin, like turning a doorknob or a steering wheel. Torque = force x distance from the spinning point, so pushing farther from the center twists harder.
terms.angular velocity: How fast something spins, and around which axis, measured in radians per second. 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians per second is one full turn every second.
terms.radians: Another way to measure angles. A full circle is 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians, which is 360 degrees. `math.rad(90)` turns 90 degrees into radians.
terms.anchored: An anchored part is frozen in place. Physics and constraint forces cannot move it. Set `part.Anchored = false` if you want a constraint to move it.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.restitution: Bounciness, from 0 (no bounce, just stops) to 1 (bounces back as hard as it hit).
terms.actuator: The part of a constraint that powers movement by itself, like a motor. ActuatorType picks None (no power), Motor (keep spinning/moving at a speed) or Servo (move to a target spot and stop).
terms.motor (ActuatorType): Keeps turning or sliding at a set speed, like a fan or a car wheel.
terms.servo (ActuatorType): Moves to a set target angle or position and holds there, like a robot arm or an automatic door.
terms.limits: Stops that keep a joint from moving too far, like a door that can only swing 90 degrees.
terms.acceleration: How fast speed changes. The rule is F = m x a (force = mass x acceleration). Push a mass-5.6 part with force 56 and it speeds up by 10 studs/s every second.
terms.world space: Directions measured using the whole game world's fixed arrows: Y is always straight up toward the sky, no matter how a part is turned.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) bundled together. Used for positions, directions, forces and speeds. Y is up.
terms.linear: In a straight line (sliding), as opposed to angular (spinning).
terms.inclination angle: How tilted the spin line is compared to the slide line, from -180 to 180 degrees. 0 means they point the same way.
terms.degrees: The usual way to measure angles: 90 degrees is a quarter turn. TargetAngle, LowerAngle, UpperAngle and InclinationAngle use degrees.
terms.SlidingBallConstraint: The parent class this constraint gets its sliding settings from, like ActuatorType, Velocity, TargetPosition, LowerLimit and UpperLimit.

examples.title: A powered wheel with up-and-down travel
examples.code:
local cylinder = workspace:WaitForChild("Car"):WaitForChild("FrontWheel"):WaitForChild("CylindricalConstraint")

-- SPIN: drive the wheel like a motor
cylinder.AngularActuatorType = Enum.ActuatorType.Motor
cylinder.AngularVelocity = 15        -- radians per second (about 2.4 turns per second)
cylinder.MotorMaxTorque = 100000      -- enough twist to move the car

-- SLIDE: let the wheel move up and down only 1 stud each way
cylinder.LimitsEnabled = true
cylinder.LowerLimit = -1
cylinder.UpperLimit = 1
-- (a SpringConstraint between the wheel and body does the bouncing)
explain: AngularActuatorType = Motor makes the wheel keep spinning at AngularVelocity, measured in radians per second (6.28 = one turn per second).
MotorMaxTorque is the most twist the motor can use; heavy cars need more.
LimitsEnabled, LowerLimit and UpperLimit come from SlidingBallConstraint and keep the sliding within 1 stud up or down.
Add a SpringConstraint between the same parts so the wheel bounces back after bumps.

gotchas: Spinning settings start with 'Angular' (AngularActuatorType, AngularVelocity). Sliding settings (ActuatorType, Velocity, Speed) come from SlidingBallConstraint. Do not mix them up.
AngularVelocity and AngularSpeed are in radians per second, but TargetAngle and the angle limits are in degrees.
If the wheel spins the wrong way around, rotate the attachments or change InclinationAngle.

If a part is joined this way to an anchored part (or something connected to an anchored part), its physics is not calculated on the player's own device when they touch it, so it may feel slightly delayed.
